:::

::: notes
~2 min, setting the stage with history. Two years ago — late 2024 — the way most of us touched
these models was this: a chatbot in a browser tab. The model was already smart, and the smart thing
to do was to treat it as an oracle: ask it for the code, then carry the intelligence out through the
clipboard, into your editor, where you fixed the imports, ran it, read the traceback, and went back
to ask again. Every loop through the problem passed through your hands. The model thought; you did
everything else. Hold onto that division of labor — the whole history I want to tell you is the
story of that division dissolving.
:::


## The first "agents" were hand-wired DAGs {#dag-era}

::: {style="display:flex;justify-content:center;align-items:center;gap:60px;margin-top:60px"}
![](images/openai-agent-builder-dag.jpeg){style="width:1150px;border:2px solid #C5B89E;border-radius:10px"}
:::

::: {style="text-align:center;margin-top:26px"}
[intelligence in the boxes · plumbing between]{style="color:#7A6F5C;font-size:0.85em"}
:::

::: notes
Then came the first things called agents — and they looked like this. This is OpenAI's Agent
Builder, from about a year and a half ago. Look at it: it's a DAG. A query-rewrite node, a
classifier node, an if/else, two specialist LLM nodes, an end state. This should feel like home —
it's a pipeline, and pipelines are this room's native language. And that's exactly why I show it:
the human encodes the control flow, and the LLM calls sit inside the boxes. Intelligence in the
boxes, plumbing between. When people in 2024 said "agents are brittle," this is the architecture
they were describing — and if your intuitions about agents were formed here, they are due for an
update, because this picture is already obsolete.
:::


## A harness inverts the picture: control flow lives in the model {#harness}

::: {style="display:flex;justify-content:center;margin-top:30px"}
```{=html}
<video data-autoplay loop muted playsinline src="images/earendil-harness.mp4" style="width:1180px;border-radius:10px"></video>
```
:::

::: {style="text-align:center;margin-top:24px"}
[system prompt · tools · agentic loop · translation layer — [earendil.com/posts/what-is-a-harness](https://earendil.com/posts/what-is-a-harness/)]{style="color:#7A6F5C;font-size:0.8em"}
:::

::: notes
The modern form is called a harness, and it deletes the DAG. Four components — watch them build: a
system prompt that says who the agent is; tools — read a file, run a command, search — described to
the model; an agentic loop; and a translation layer to the model's API. That's the whole
architecture. The model chooses tools and loops until the task is done. Nobody draws the graph — the
model decides, at every step, what happens next. The control flow moved out of the boxes-and-arrows
and into the model itself. This is what the word "agentic" actually means, and it's why the
brittleness went away: there is no pipeline to break. Claude Code, Codex, and every serious coding
agent today is this — a few hundred lines of harness around a very capable model.
:::

```
:::

::: notes
So here is the inversion, side by side, and it's the one mental move I need from you this morning.
On the left, the world your pipeline intuitions were built for: you draw the graph, the
intelligence sits in the boxes. On the right, today: the model sits in a loop with tools — and the
graph didn't vanish, it moved. The model draws it, for this task, on the fly: it decides to fan
out three sub-agents, to put a verifier behind two of them, to run a pipeline — and when the task
is done that graph is thrown away. Nobody could have drawn it in advance because it depends on
what the model finds as it goes. If you internalize just this one picture, the rest
of the talk — and honestly, the rest of the next few years — will make much more sense. Everything
I'll show you in the tutorial is this right-hand picture, pointed at a cosmology problem.
:::

::: notes
~1.5 min. [DRAFT — refine to your voice.] Here's what "the model draws the graph" looks like in
practice, because it's very concrete. An orchestrating agent holds the plan and the judgement.
When it hits a sub-goal that would flood its own context — read two thousand lines of a paper,
implement a module, sweep a directory — it *spawns a subagent*: a fresh model instance, its own
clean context window, given one job, returning a summary. Each blue bar is a separate context.
The orchestrator's own window stays lean — just the management view — which is what lets one
session carry an arc that used to take five. And when the model wants structure it can write a
*workflow*: a small pipeline — review for bugs, fan out two independent verifiers, keep only the
confirmed findings — composed for this task and discarded after. That's a DAG. It just wasn't
drawn by you. Two things I want you to notice, because they'll come back in the tutorial. First,
this is context architecture before it's parallelism: the reason to split is that each piece
wants a clean window. Second, look where verification appears — as nodes the model added on its
own. When we get to the practice at scale, "design the checks into the work" is exactly this
picture, made deliberate.
:::

<rect x="900" y="560" width="40" height="26" rx="5" fill="#BC4538" fill-opacity="0.9"/><text x="955" y="582" fill="#1B1611">new tokens · computed this step</text>

```
:::

::: {style="text-align:center;margin-top:26px;color:#7A6F5C;font-size:0.8em"}
[design rule: stable system prompt first · append-only history · never edit the middle]{style="font-family:'IBM Plex Mono',monospace;font-size:0.85em"}
:::

::: notes
~1.5 min. One piece of mechanics before we move on, because it's the thing that makes the loop on
the previous slide economically possible — and it's the single most important thing to understand
about how these systems are priced and engineered. The model is stateless. Every step of the loop,
the harness sends the *entire* context again: system prompt, tool definitions, the whole
conversation so far, plus the new tool result. Naively that's quadratic — a hundred-step task
re-reads a hundred-thousand-token context a hundred times. What saves it is prompt caching: the
provider keeps the model's internal state for a prefix it has already processed, so if this step's
context begins with exactly the same tokens as the last one — and in a loop it does — the whole
prefix is served from cache. Cached tokens cost about a tenth as much and skip the prefill
latency; only the tail — the newest tool result and the model's new output — is actually computed.
[Point at the rows: the hatched region grows, the red stays small.] Two consequences. For cost:
a long agentic session is dominated by cache reads, which is why it's affordable at all. For
design: everything in the harness is organised to keep the prefix stable — the system prompt
goes first and never changes, history is append-only, you never edit the middle of the context.
That's the design rule at the bottom, and once you know it you'll recognise it everywhere in how
these tools behave — why they compact context rather than reorder it, why long stable instructions
are cheap and mid-conversation changes aren't. Hold onto it; it's what makes the tutorial's
twenty-minute session cost cents.
:::

::: notes
Now let me place us in time — and this is a plot a cosmologist can't resist. Take the big
transitions in the history of complexity and plot them on a log axis of time before present: Earth,
four and a half billion years; anatomically modern humans, three hundred thousand; agriculture, ten
thousand; industry, three hundred; computers, eighty; large language models, eight. Roughly evenly
spaced — in log time. Each transition arrives an order of magnitude faster than the last. Extrapolate
the series and the spacing goes to zero in finite time: the math predicts a singularity. Now,
extrapolation is exactly the kind of move this audience is trained to distrust, and rightly so. So
let me give you something much more concrete than a log plot.

This is Stripe — the payments company, one of the most sober, numbers-driven institutions in the
economy — writing to its investors two weeks ago. They declared that January 1st, 2026 marked the
beginning of the singularity, and that they have been operating on that basis since. Not as
futurism — as an operational reading of their own data: an inflection in new-firm creation, revenue
up forty-one percent year over year, nearly the entire Forbes AI 50 running on their rails. The
word "singularity" is migrating from speculation to descriptive vocabulary — serious people now use
it to describe the present. I can't tell you what it means from the inside — that's rather the
point of the word — but I can tell you what it means for us: these are the very last years of the
old way of doing science, and the very first years of the new. That's the frame for everything
that follows: what does the new way actually look like, at a keyboard, on a real problem?
:::


<!-- ═══════════════ BEAT 3 · THE TUTORIAL: measure dark energy ═══════════════ -->

## Measure dark energy in twenty minutes {.section-divider #tutorial-open}

::: {style="text-align:center;margin-top:60px"}
[580 supernovae · one parameter · one agent]{style="color:#7A6F5C;font-size:0.9em"}
:::

::: {style="text-align:center;margin-top:40px"}
[lightconeresearch.github.io/agent-skills → ASTRA]{style="font-family:'IBM Plex Mono',monospace;font-size:0.6em;color:#7A6F5C"}
:::

::: notes
So here's the tutorial — and everything I'm about to show you is public, linked at the bottom, and
designed so you can run it yourself this afternoon. The problem is a classic: use the relation
between the brightness and redshift of Type Ia supernovae to measure the dark energy content of the
universe — the same measurement that won the 2011 Nobel Prize. Five hundred and eighty supernovae,
one free parameter, one agent. Mechanically it's a least-squares fit; that's deliberate — the
physics is simple enough that you can watch the *practice* instead. And the practice is the point:
you'll see the agent do the work, and you'll see the thing I actually care about, which is how the
record of that work gets kept honest.
:::


## A skill is expertise the agent loads on demand {#skills}

::: {style="display:flex;justify-content:center;align-items:flex-start;gap:50px;margin-top:20px"}
::: {style="width:46%"}
```yaml
# astra/skills/astra/SKILL.md
---
name: astra
description: >
  ASTRA (astra.yaml) support: what the format
  is, and how to drive the `astra` CLI. Invoke
  whenever reading, writing, validating, or
  restructuring an astra.yaml spec …
---
# ASTRA
## What ASTRA is
## Orient before authoring
## Citations, quotes, and supporting evidence
## CLI reference          … 108 lines
```
```text
astra/
├── skills/astra/SKILL.md     the expertise
├── hooks/hooks.json          validate on save
└── scripts/                  the checks
```
:::
::: {style="width:50%"}
```{=html}
<svg viewBox="0 0 800 560" style="width:100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
  <defs><marker id="sk" markerWidth="12" markerHeight="12" refX="8" refY="5" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z" fill="#BC4538"/></marker></defs>

  <text x="90" y="300" font-family="EB Garamond, serif" font-size="26" fill="#BC4538" font-weight="600">loaded on demand — the whole SKILL.md</text>
  <g font-family="IBM Plex Mono, monospace" font-size="20" fill="#1B1611">
    <text x="90" y="338">what counts as a decision · how to parameterise</text>
    <text x="90" y="366">when to split an analysis · how to cite evidence</text>
    <text x="90" y="394">→ behaves like someone who read the docs</text>
  </g>
  <!-- hooks -->
  <rect x="60" y="440" width="680" height="90" rx="12" fill="#F4ECDC" stroke="#3F8278" stroke-width="2.5" stroke-dasharray="8 6"/>
  <text x="90" y="476" font-family="EB Garamond, serif" font-size="26" fill="#3F8278" font-weight="600">hooks — deterministic, outside the model</text>

</svg>
```
:::
:::

::: notes
~1.5 min. [DRAFT — refine to your voice.] One last piece of the harness before the tutorial,
because the tutorial's first move is "install a plugin" and I want that to mean something. A
skill is a markdown file. That's it — a `SKILL.md` with a name, a one-paragraph description of
*when* it applies, and a body that is the expertise: for ASTRA, what counts as a decision, how to
parameterise a choice, when to split an analysis, how to cite evidence so it can be verified. The
mechanism is progressive disclosure. The agent's context always carries the *index* — one line per
skill, name plus trigger — and nothing more; that's cheap, and it's in the cached prefix. When
your request matches — "set up an astra.yaml" — the whole body is loaded, and from that moment
the agent behaves like someone who has read the documentation. This is how a general model becomes
a domain expert without retraining: the expertise lives in a file you can read, diff, and version.
And a plugin is a skill plus hooks — small deterministic scripts that fire on events, outside the
model. The astra plugin has one that runs `astra validate` every time the spec is saved. The model
can't forget to do it, because the model isn't the one doing it. Hold that pattern: expertise in a
file the model reads on demand, checks in a script the model can't skip. Everything in the
tutorial is those two things pointed at a supernova catalogue.
:::


## ASTRA records the analysis; the agent does the work {#astra-intro}

::: {style="display:flex;justify-content:center;align-items:center;gap:90px;margin-top:90px"}
::: {style="width:44%"}
```yaml
# astra.yaml — machine-readable record
inputs:      # what goes in
outputs:     # what comes out
recipes:     # how, exactly
decisions:   # the choices that matter
evidence:    # verified against sources
```
:::
::: {style="width:40%"}
```bash
uv tool install astra-tools

claude plugin install \
  astra@lightcone-research
```
:::
:::

::: notes
Two pieces of infrastructure, both installable in one line. ASTRA is a format — a YAML file that
is a machine-readable record of an analysis: its inputs, its outputs, the recipes that connect
them, and — the part I'll spend the most time on — the consequential methodological decisions, with
evidence that gets verified against the literature. ASTRA runs nothing; it validates and inspects.
The runner is the agent — the harness you just met. And the plugin teaches your agent the format:
the judgment about what counts as a decision, how to parameterize choices, when to split an
analysis. You install these two things, start your agent in an empty directory, and everything from
here on is prompts.
:::


## 1 · The data — you ask; the agent fetches and reads {#step-data}

::: {.live-pair}
::: {.live-left}
::: {.prompt-card}
Download the Union2.1 supernova compilation from the Supernova Cosmology Project into a `data/`
directory:

`https://supernova.lbl.gov/Union/figures/SCPUnion2.1_mu_vs_z.txt`

Then show me the first few rows and tell me what's in the file.
:::
:::
::: {.live-right}
::: {.watch-head}
while it runs — what to look for
:::
::: {.watch-row}
[supernovae]{.k} [580 SNe Ia]{.v}
:::
::: {.watch-row}
[redshift range]{.k} [z = 0.015 – 1.414]{.v}
:::
::: {.watch-row}
[columns]{.k} [name · z · μ · σ~μ~ · P(low-mass host)]{.v}
:::
::: {.watch-row}
[header]{.k} [M(h=0.7) — calibration lives here]{.v}
:::
::: {.watch-row}
[the tell]{.k} [does the agent *read the header*?]{.v}
:::
:::
:::

::: notes
Step one. This block is a prompt — you paste it into the agent, not the shell. Everything in this
tutorial in this style is words addressed to the agent, and that's the first thing to notice about
the practice: the interface is intent. The agent downloads the Union2.1 compilation — the 2012
supernova sample — reads the header, and tells you what's there: five hundred eighty supernovae,
redshifts from 0.015 to 1.4, distance moduli carrying an h equals 0.7 calibration from the header.
Note that it read the header and told us about the calibration — hold that thought, because the
header is going to matter again at the end.
:::


## 2 · The spec — say what the analysis is {#step-spec}

::: {.live-pair}
::: {.live-left}
::: {.prompt-card}
Use the astra skill to set up an `astra.yaml` for this. I want to fit a flat LCDM model to this
data to recover Omega_Lambda, varying only Omega_Lambda and using the metadata in the file's
header.

Two outputs: the best fit, and a downstream best-fit Hubble diagram figure with an absolute panel
and a residuals panel. Put outputs under `results/`, e.g. `results/hubble_diagram.png`.

In this first pass, let's only use inputs, outputs, and recipes. Please walk me through each
element that you add.
:::
:::
::: {.live-right}
::: {.watch-head}
while it runs — the shape the hook will validate
:::
```yaml
inputs:
  - id: union21
    type: data
    source: data/SCPUnion2.1_mu_vs_z.txt

outputs:
  - id: best_fit
    type: metric
    inputs: [union21]
    recipe:
      command: python src/fit.py
        --data {inputs.union21} --out {output}
  - id: hubble_diagram
    type: figure
    inputs: [union21, best_fit]
    recipe:
      command: python src/plot_hubble.py …
```
:::
:::

::: notes
Step two: say what the analysis is, in words, and the agent writes the spec. Inputs: the data file.
Outputs: a best-fit — Omega Lambda with uncertainty, chi-squared — and a Hubble-diagram figure
downstream of it. Each output carries a recipe: the exact command that produces it, with the
dependencies explicit. Notice what this is: it's a DAG again! — but look who drew it. You said four
sentences of intent; the model wrote the graph, and a hook validated the file the moment it was
saved. The graph didn't disappear from science — provenance still wants a graph — it moved from
being the thing you hand-wire to being an artifact the agent maintains.
:::


## 3 · Run it — the agent implements, executes, and reports {#step-run}

::: {.live-pair}
::: {.live-left}
::: {.prompt-card}
Use uv to set up a virtual environment and install any needed packages.

Then implement the analysis. Write the scripts the recipes call, run them, and show me the Hubble
diagram. Save the figure to `results/hubble_diagram.png`.
:::

::: {style="margin-top:40px;text-align:center"}
[expect one number]{style="color:#7A6F5C;font-size:0.7em"}<br>
[Ω~Λ~ ≈ 0.72]{.stat-hero style="font-size:1.4em"}
:::
:::
::: {.live-right}
::: {.watch-head}
live — fills in when the agent writes the file
:::
::: {.live-figure data-src="results/hubble_diagram.png"}
:::
:::
:::

::: notes
Step three: run it. One prompt: set up the environment, write the scripts the recipes call, run
them, show me the figure. The agent writes the fitter, writes the plotting script, runs both, and
one number comes back: Omega Lambda equals 0.722 plus or minus 0.013. Seventy-two percent of the
universe is dark energy — measured, from a standing start, in about five minutes of wall-clock
time. If we stopped here, this would be a cute demo: agent fits line, film at eleven. But this is
where the scientific part actually starts — because how do you know that number is right?
:::


## 4 · Check it — the quote is verified against the paper itself {#step-verify}

::: {.live-pair}
::: {.live-left}
::: {.prompt-card}
The paper that published this catalogue is Suzuki et al. 2012, arXiv 1105.3470. Cache the paper,
verify their own Omega_Lambda from these supernovae, and show me the output. Then record it in
`astra.yaml` as a prior insight with the quote as evidence, and tell me how our constraint compares
to theirs.
:::
:::
::: {.live-right}
::: {.watch-head}
while it runs — what a verified claim looks like
:::
```yaml
prior_insights:
  suzuki_2012_result:
    claim: >
      Omega_Lambda = 0.705 (+0.040, -0.043)
      including systematic errors.
    evidence:
      - doi: "10.48550/arXiv.1105.3470"
        quote:
          exact: "… ΩΛ = 0.705+0.040−0.043
          including systematics"
        location: { value: "page=17" }
```
```text
$ astra validate astra.yaml --verify-evidence
✓ Quote verified on page(s) [17]
```
::: {style="margin-top:14px;text-align:center;font-size:0.75em;color:#7A6F5C"}
theirs ± 0.04 · ours ± 0.013 — same 580 supernovae. *Too* confident.
:::
:::
:::

::: notes
Step four: check it against the paper that published this catalogue — Suzuki et al. 2012. And
here's my favorite mechanism in the whole system. The agent caches the paper and records the
published constraint as a *prior insight* — a claim with evidence. The evidence is an exact quote,
with a page number — and ASTRA searches the cached PDF and verifies that the quote actually appears
on page seventeen. This matters because agents, like graduate students, occasionally remember
papers saying things they don't say. Claims about the literature are grounded in the literature,
mechanically. And with the quote verified, we can compare: they got 0.705, plus 0.040 minus 0.043.
Our central value agrees nicely. But look at the error bars — ours are three times tighter, on the
same 580 supernovae. Same data, same model. Something is wrong, and it's wrong in the direction
that should scare you: we're *too* confident.
:::


## 5 · One decision doubles the error bar {#step-decision}

::: {.live-pair}
::: {.live-left}
::: {.prompt-card}
Let's understand why our error bars are so much tighter than theirs. Download the two Union2.1
covariance files:

`https://supernova.lbl.gov/Union/figures/SCPUnion2.1_covmat_nosys.txt`<br>
`https://supernova.lbl.gov/Union/figures/SCPUnion2.1_covmat_sys.txt`

Work out which one the main data file's error column is using, then add a decision to `astra.yaml`
to switch to the other, and see what impact it has on our constraint.
:::
:::
::: {.live-right}
::: {.watch-head}
while it runs — where the three numbers land
:::
```{=html}
<svg viewBox="0 0 900 640" style="width:100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
  <text x="450" y="44" font-family="EB Garamond, serif" font-size="30" fill="#7A6F5C" text-anchor="middle" font-style="italic">the value barely moves — the honesty is in the width</text>
  <g>
    <line x1="396" y1="150" x2="523" y2="150" stroke="#BC4538" stroke-width="9" stroke-linecap="round"/>
    <circle cx="460" cy="150" r="16" fill="#BC4538"/>
    <text x="460" y="112" font-family="EB Garamond, serif" font-size="34" fill="#1B1611" text-anchor="middle">ours — statistical only · 0.722 ± 0.013</text>
  </g>
  <g>
    <line x1="275" y1="300" x2="567" y2="300" stroke="#3F8278" stroke-width="9" stroke-linecap="round"/>
    <circle cx="421" cy="300" r="16" fill="#3F8278"/>
    <text x="421" y="262" font-family="EB Garamond, serif" font-size="34" fill="#1B1611" text-anchor="middle">ours — with systematics · 0.714 ± 0.030</text>
  </g>
  <g>
    <line x1="167" y1="450" x2="572" y2="450" stroke="#3D5BA0" stroke-width="9" stroke-linecap="round"/>
    <circle cx="377" cy="450" r="16" fill="#3D5BA0"/>
    <text x="377" y="412" font-family="EB Garamond, serif" font-size="34" fill="#1B1611" text-anchor="middle">Suzuki et al. 2012 · 0.705 +0.040 −0.043</text>
  </g>
  <line x1="60" y1="540" x2="840" y2="540" stroke="#1B1611" stroke-width="3"/>
  <g font-family="IBM Plex Mono, monospace" font-size="26" fill="#7A6F5C" text-anchor="middle">
    <line x1="109" y1="540" x2="109" y2="552" stroke="#1B1611" stroke-width="2"/><text x="109" y="590">0.65</text>
    <line x1="352" y1="540" x2="352" y2="552" stroke="#1B1611" stroke-width="2"/><text x="352" y="590">0.70</text>
    <line x1="596" y1="540" x2="596" y2="552" stroke="#1B1611" stroke-width="2"/><text x="596" y="590">0.75</text>
    <line x1="840" y1="540" x2="840" y2="552" stroke="#1B1611" stroke-width="2"/><text x="840" y="590">0.80</text>
  </g>
  <text x="450" y="630" font-family="EB Garamond, serif" font-size="30" fill="#1B1611" text-anchor="middle">Ω<tspan font-size="22" dy="6">Λ</tspan></text>
</svg>
```
:::
:::

::: notes
Step five, and the payoff. We ask the agent to find out why: download the two Union2.1 covariance
files — with and without systematics — work out which one our error column corresponds to, and
record a *decision* in the spec: statistical-only versus full systematic covariance. The answer:
our fit had been using the no-systematics errors — the error column in the data file *is* the diagonal
of the no-systematics covariance, to twelve decimal places. Everything the systematic covariance knows was
sitting in a file we had never opened. Switch to it, and watch the plot: the central value barely
moves — 0.722 to 0.714 — but the uncertainty more than doubles, and only then does our measurement
actually lie beside the published one: 0.2 sigma apart, their data, their systematics, their
method. Here's the lesson, and it's the sentence I'd have you take home: if you had ranked this
choice by its effect on the best-fit number, it would have looked nearly irrelevant. It is the
difference between a number that *resembles* theirs and a number you can *put beside* theirs. That
is what a decision is — and this field, all of science, is made of thousands of them, almost none
of them written down. ASTRA writes them down.
:::


## Three more decisions are still sitting in this analysis {#going-further}

::: {style="display:flex;justify-content:center;gap:70px;margin-top:130px;text-align:center"}
::: {.decision-chip}
optimiser<br>[likely a null result — worth recording as one]{.chip-sub}
:::
::: {.decision-chip}
redshift range<br>[longest lever arm, worst systematics]{.chip-sub}
:::
::: {.decision-chip}
dark-energy model<br>[hold w = −1, or fit it]{.chip-sub}
:::
:::

::: notes
And the tutorial ends by pointing at what it didn't do: three more decisions sitting in this little
analysis, unimplemented. The optimiser — likely a null result, and a null result is worth recording
as one. The redshift range — the high-z supernovae carry the longest lever arm and the worst
systematics. And the dark-energy model itself: hold w at minus one, or fit it and buy a degeneracy.
Each is one more option, one more recipe argument, one more reason written down. That's a toy
analysis. Now scale the picture up: a real weak-lensing analysis has hundreds of these decisions
and takes a collaboration five years. What does this practice look like there? That's the last
part of the tutorial — how this works day to day, on real science.
:::

## Stable principles are emerging for agentic science {#principles}

:::::::::::::: {.columns style="margin-top:2.6em;width:calc(100% + 208px);margin-left:-104px"}

::: {.column style="width:27%;text-align:center;padding:0 1em"}
::: {style="font-size:1.3em;font-weight:600;color:#bc4538"}
Verification
:::
::: {style="margin-top:0.35em;font-size:0.86em;color:#3a342b;line-height:1.42;text-wrap:balance"}
design checks into the work
:::
:::

::: {.column style="width:46%;text-align:center;padding:0 0.8em;border-left:1px solid #d9cdb4"}
::: {style="font-size:1.3em;font-weight:600;color:#bc4538"}
Looping
:::
::: {style="margin-top:0.35em;font-size:0.86em;color:#3a342b;line-height:1.42"}
towards a desired state<br>a constitution rather than a plan
:::
:::

::: {.column style="width:27%;text-align:center;padding:0 1em;border-left:1px solid #d9cdb4"}
::: {style="font-size:1.3em;font-weight:600;color:#bc4538"}
Accumulation
:::
::: {style="margin-top:0.35em;font-size:0.86em;color:#3a342b;line-height:1.42;text-wrap:balance"}
searchable traces of previous work
:::
:::

::::::::::::::

::: {style="text-align:center;margin-top:2.4em"}
```{=html}
<div class="r-stack" style="justify-items:center">
<pre class="fragment fade-out" data-fragment-index="1" style="display:inline-block;justify-self:center;text-align:left;background:#FBF6E9;border:1px solid #C5B89E;border-radius:14px;padding:0.8em 1.5em;font-family:'IBM Plex Mono',ui-monospace,monospace;font-size:0.72em;line-height:1.6;color:#3a342b;box-shadow:0 1px 5px rgba(0,0,0,0.05);width:fit-content;margin:0 auto"><span style="color:#7a6f5c"># an agent is an LLM in a loop</span>
<span style="color:#3F8278">context</span> = startup_context + user_prompt
<span style="color:#bc4538">while</span> <span style="color:#bc4538">not</span> done:
    response = llm(<span style="color:#3F8278">context</span>)
    <span style="color:#3F8278">context</span> += execute(response.tool_calls)</pre>
<pre class="fragment" data-fragment-index="1" style="display:inline-block;justify-self:center;text-align:left;background:#FBF6E9;border:1px solid #C5B89E;border-radius:14px;padding:0.8em 1.5em;font-family:'IBM Plex Mono',ui-monospace,monospace;font-size:0.72em;line-height:1.6;color:#3a342b;box-shadow:0 1px 5px rgba(0,0,0,0.05);width:fit-content;margin:0 auto"><span style="color:#7a6f5c"># the same loop, around whole sessions</span>
<span style="color:#3F8278">constitution</span> = user_intent
<span style="color:#bc4538">while</span> <span style="color:#bc4538">not</span> done:
    state = get_state(environment, <span style="color:#3F8278">constitution</span>)  <span style="color:#7a6f5c"># unbiased assessment of state</span>
    implement(state, <span style="color:#3F8278">constitution</span>)
    amend(<span style="color:#3F8278">constitution</span>)  <span style="color:#7a6f5c"># open-ended research</span></pre>
</div>
```
:::

::: notes
~2 min. [Lifted from the CNRS deck — Cail's rehearsed script, lightly retargeted.] The specific
techniques change every month as the models get better — what I did last July looks nothing like
what I do now. But underneath that churn, three principles have stayed stable. These are what I'd
teach.

**Verify.** The moment agents can do a lot, verification becomes the bottleneck — you can generate
far more than you can check. So you organize the work around making the checks cheap and
high-signal, and more fundamentally you design the work so the checks are built in. Tests are the
obvious case — but real science has no ground truth to test against; the data is real, the answer
is unknown, and a "check" can be a subtle, nuanced judgment. You saw a small version in the
tutorial: the verified quote, the recorded decision. At scale it becomes a design problem: name the
things that must be true if the work is right, and check them as you go.

**Loop toward a desired state.** The central object is the loop. An agent just is an LLM in a
loop — act, observe, update, repeat. The next level of abstraction is to put a loop around whole
sessions: each one starts from a fresh context. And what you hand each session matters: for
open-ended research, a rigid plan is often counterproductive — it forces you to foresee everything
and can't adapt to what the results tell you. Instead you write a constitution: it describes the
desired state; the current state is discoverable from the environment. A goal to reach, not a plan
to follow. Notice this is the same inversion as the harness slide — you stop drawing the graph at
the session level too.

**Accumulate context.** You quickly start doing more than you can possibly remember — what you've
already checked, what's true, what failed. You have to take notes, and you can't do it by hand. So
you need a memory system: as much context as possible in a form that's searchable, with progressive
disclosure — summaries that open into detail. This is what keeps the work honest: it's how you
avoid hallucinating, and how you know what ground you've already covered.

If you remember three things: verification, looping, accumulation.
:::


## Moving from chats to long-horizon tasks {#longhorizon-tasks}

<div class="r-stack" style="margin-top:0.3em;width:calc(100% + 208px);margin-left:-104px"><img src="images/agentic_task_board.png" class="no-treat fragment fade-out" data-fragment-index="1" style="width:100%;max-width:none;border-radius:6px;box-shadow:0 12px 34px rgba(27,22,17,0.22)"><img src="images/agentic_task_report.png" class="no-treat fragment" data-fragment-index="1" style="max-width:100%;max-height:840px;border-radius:6px;box-shadow:0 12px 34px rgba(27,22,17,0.22)"></div>

::: notes
~1 min. [Lifted from CNRS; retargeted — DRAFT, refine to your voice.] Here's what the looping
principle looks like in my actual working day. Early on I worked the way everyone does — one prompt
at a time, steering each step myself. Now I mostly hand agents long-horizon tasks and let them run.
This is my real task board: each card is an agent working a piece of the analysis on its own — some
drafting, some in flight, some waiting on my review. And when one finishes — [advance] — it hands
back a full write-up of a real result: here a shear-catalog cross-check, figures and numbers ready
for me to check. My job moved up a level: from doing each step to designing the tasks and verifying
what comes back. The constitutions those agents run on are exactly the astra.yaml idea grown up:
specs that describe the desired state of a piece of science.
:::

![](images/cosebis_bsigma_talk.png){.blend-figure width=92% fig-align="center"}

::: notes
~2 min. [Lifted from CNRS — Cail's rehearsed script, with a two-sentence setup added for a room that
hasn't seen the UNIONS science; DRAFT the setup in your own words.] Here's what verification looks
like on the real thing. Setup, in two sentences: gravitational lensing distorts galaxy shapes in a
pattern that has no curl — physics forbids the swirling "B-mode" — so any B-mode we measure has to be
contamination, and hunting it is the daily craft of the field. We measure it three independent ways
— correlation functions in configuration space, power spectra in harmonic space, and COSEBIs, the
sharp discrete modes both of those compress into — and with agents doing the labor, we could afford
to run all three, with full covariances, on every version of the catalogue.

Now the plot. Don't read the axes; read the shape. On the left, points that should sit on the flat
line instead climb away from it: a swirl that physics forbids, so it *must* be contamination. Two of
our three measures had passed; this third, sharper one caught it, because it concentrates a small
fingerprint the others dilute below notice. We could even pin down its size — it repeats at the
spacing of the camera's individual sensors, a man-made scale where the instrument would imprint
itself. Right panel: after we cut the affected range, it sits back on the line. The move to land:
the disagreement isn't a failure of the analysis, it's the analysis *working* — the measurement
telling us where the instrument was lying. And this is the honest version of "agents help": not
doing the same analysis faster, but doing a *more rigorous* one, because you can now check at a
finer level than any human team could afford.
:::

measured honestly, plus the practice that drove it. I started doing this work with agents in July
2025 — the shaded era. The honest measure of work isn't net lines (they cancel) or commit counts
(gameable); it's everything I touched, written plus deleted. By that measure 2026 Q1 is
twenty-two thousand lines even though it nets to almost zero, because agentic work is relentless
iteration and refactoring. My output grew roughly six-fold and came to match my three closest
collaborators combined — one person doing the work of a small team. And the row below is the
practice I built as I went, on the same timeline: loops, then a memory system, then constitutions,
then the move from chat sessions to autonomous tasks, and finally Lightcone — the open ecosystem
where tools like ASTRA live. This chart is the talk's title made concrete: the labor scales.

practice".] This is how it all composes, as a flywheel. I pour in what a cosmologist knows — but
collaboratively: meeting transcripts, the team's vetted wikis, shared judgment. That becomes the
objectives and the verification pressure that shape a funnel; inside it, long-horizon agent loops
do an enormous amount of labor without drifting. Out come live reports I can actually read and
check — and the best of what I learn flows back into the expertise that steers the next turn. A
small amount of human judgment, encoded and refined each cycle, steers a vast amount of machine
labor toward results I can stand behind. That's what made a small team's analysis tractable this
year — and it's the shape I think scientific collaborations drift toward generally. Which brings
us to what this means for all of us.
:::

## Astrophysics has become an information science {#ball-1}

::: {style="display:flex;justify-content:center;margin-top:110px"}
::: {.quote-card style="max-width:1400px"}
"…if every current prosumer-tier subscriber to codex and claude code donated a tiny share of their
monthly compute, **we will soon be able to automate more astrophysics than is currently done by
human astrophysicists** — the ones who operate in the 'astrophysics as data science' regime at
least."

::: {.quote-attrib}
Dean W. Ball — August 8, 2026
:::
:::
:::

::: notes
So what does it mean? Let me borrow two claims from Dean Ball — a policy researcher, not an AI
booster — writing three weeks ago. First claim: some sciences, astrophysics chief among them, have
in practice become information sciences — high-capex shared instruments producing data, plus labor
that is almost entirely computation on that data. And in that regime, the arithmetic is brutal: the
idle compute of the world's coding-agent subscribers is soon enough to automate more astrophysics
than human astrophysicists currently do. You just watched the existence proof: a dark-energy
measurement, spec'd, run, verified against the literature, by an agent, in minutes. He's talking
about us. This is coming right for our field, and I think both of his claims are true.
:::


## The meta-skill: knowing what is computationally tractable {#ball-2}

::: {style="display:flex;justify-content:center;margin-top:110px"}
::: {.quote-card style="max-width:1400px"}
"if you can master the meta-skill of figuring out what problems in arbitrary domains are
computationally tractable … you'll have refined heuristics for the right questions to ask about
everything. … **this is probably the skill to have optimized for** … though I readily admit I don't
know how long it will remain a human advantage. **it is for now though.**"

::: {.quote-attrib}
Dean W. Ball — August 8, 2026
:::
:::
:::

::: notes
Second claim, and this one is about you. The scarce skill in this regime is not coding and it's
not prompting — it's the meta-skill of looking at an arbitrary domain and knowing which of its
problems are computationally tractable, and what question to ask to make progress along the
margin. Master that and you get to be, in his phrase, a kind of meta-genius — for at least a year
or two, maybe longer. Everyone in this room is unusually well positioned for this: physics-informed
ML is *already* the discipline of knowing what physics can be pushed through computation. But
notice the honesty of the last clause: he doesn't know how long it remains a human advantage. It is
for now. The meta-skill is temporary — and that's not a reason for despair, it's a reason for
urgency and, honestly, for joy: this is the window in which knowing how to do this makes you
extraordinary.
:::

::: notes
~1.5 min. [Lifted from CNRS `#sim-bench-rl` — retargeted from "my program" to "what this room can
do"; DRAFT, refine to your voice.] And here is where the meta-skill lands on *this* room
specifically. The first places AI got genuinely productive were the verifiable ones — code, math —
because you can check the answer and train on it at scale. Physics has no answer key: one universe,
no re-runs. But look at what you already build. Top row: full-physics simulations, fast surrogates,
simulation-based inference — a mature ecosystem whose whole purpose is to run the analysis on a
universe whose answer we *do* know. [advance] That is exactly the substrate agents are missing.
Your expertise and your simulations become benchmarks that characterise real scientific work;
instantiated in simulation, where the truth is known, they become RL environments — a reward to
train agents on. And it flows back: every environment is traceable to the people it came from, so
the value returns to its source rather than to whoever has the most compute. Two things to say out
loud for an ML audience. First, the reward is sparse and *noisy* — you can do everything right and
still land two sigma off by chance; learning efficiently from a reward that noisy is a real, open
AI problem, and physics is the place to crack it. Second, everything is hackable, this included —
the fix isn't an unhackable reward, it's closing the sim-to-real gap so the local hacking stays
honest. Physics-informed ML is not a consumer of this transition. It is the supply chain.
:::


## The stake in the ground {#stake}

::: {style="display:flex;justify-content:center;align-items:center;margin-top:160px"}
::: {style="max-width:1400px;text-align:center;font-size:1.35em;line-height:1.45"}
In five years, I expect frontier AI to be **better at astrophysics and cosmology than the vast
majority of currently employed astrophysicists and cosmologists** — to the extent that the
economics of our field are drastically changed.
:::
:::

::: notes
So let me put a stake in the ground — a concrete, falsifiable position you can hold me to. In five
years, I expect frontier AI to be better at astrophysics and cosmology than the vast majority of
currently employed astrophysicists and cosmologists — to the point that the economics of our field
are drastically changed. I might be wrong! It's a prediction, and predictions about exponentials
are hard in both directions. But notice that everything you saw today — the harness, the tutorial,
the verified analysis — is the *current* state, the worst it will ever be. If you think I'm wrong,
I'd genuinely love to argue about it in the discussion. If I'm right, then the interesting question
isn't whether — it's what you personally do about it.
:::


## Pharmakon: we get to choose what science becomes {#pharmakon .vcenter}

:::::::::::::: {.columns style="margin-top:0.85em;align-items:stretch"}
::: {.column style="width:50%"}

::: {style="height:100%;display:flex;flex-direction:column;justify-content:space-between;padding:0.2em 1em;border-left:5px solid #7a6f5c"}
[**AI science factories**]{style="font-size:1.08em"}

::: {style="text-align:center"}

![](images/parallel_arxiv.png){.no-treat style="width:94%;border-radius:5px;box-shadow:0 8px 20px rgba(27,22,17,0.18);margin-top:0.22em"}
:::

::: {style="line-height:1.35"}
[alienation from scientific labor]{style="color:#bc4538;font-size:1.0em"}<br>
[discovery scales with capital, not expertise]{style="color:#bc4538;font-size:0.9em"}
:::

:::
::: {.column style="width:50%"}

::: {style="height:100%;display:flex;flex-direction:column;padding:0.2em 1.1em;border-left:5px solid #3F8278"}
[**An economy of contribution**]{style="font-size:1.08em;color:#3F8278"}

::: {style="flex:1;display:flex;flex-direction:column;justify-content:center;color:#1B1611;padding-bottom:2.5em"}
[« …l'augmentation du savoir des travailleurs à travers un nouvel agencement entre la machine et le travailleur »]{style="display:block;text-align:center;font-size:0.98em;line-height:1.5;padding:0 0.2em"}

[— Bernard Stiegler]{style="display:block;text-align:right;color:#3F8278;font-size:0.9em;letter-spacing:0.02em;margin-top:0.55em"}
:::
:::

:::
::::::::::::::

::: notes
~1.5 min. [Lifted from CNRS `#the-choice` — the frame is a DRAFT for you to make your own; the
first-person passage at the end is yours, keep verbatim.] Before I put the choice to you personally,
the collective version — and I get to use a Greek word in Crete. *Pharmakon*: the remedy that is
also the poison, one dose, both faces at once. Which face science gets is not decided by the
technology; it's decided by the practice we build around it.

The poison — "AI science factories." Not hypothetical: papers already framed as *Competing with AI
Scientists*, the John Henry race humans are built to lose; a *Parallel ArXiv* where agents write the
papers and agents review them — a literature with no one in it. What's lost isn't jobs, it's the
*doing* of science. And a structural loss underneath: once people are out of the loop, output is a
function of capital — the labs have every incentive to stop selling the tools and do the science
in-house. Discovery scales with capital, not expertise.

The cure — same tools, different practice. The grunt work goes to the agents; the human is freed for
the science that matters — you talk to the model, it hands you a plot, you argue about it with a
colleague on a walk, and the argument becomes the next set of actions. Not agent fleets replacing
people, not the lone genius — networks of humans amplified by agents. Stiegler called it an
*économie de la contribution*: the machine augments the worker's knowledge rather than displacing it.

[Cail's, verbatim:] This is not only about jobs. It is about keeping the part of the work we
actually love — discovery. I would far rather spend this era in wonderful, beautiful discovery,
amplified, than watch the work get slowly ripped from our hands by agent "competitors." If a day
comes when there is nothing left for us to add, so be it — but I would rather enjoy the good times
while they last, and shape the practice so people stay *in* it.
:::


## The choice is genuinely open — and neither path is bad {#choice}

::: {style="display:flex;justify-content:center;margin-top:150px"}
```{=html}
<svg viewBox="0 0 1560 580" style="width:1650px" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
  <!-- left: eddy -->
  <g>
    <path d="M 390 260 a 120 120 0 1 1 -6 -62" fill="none" stroke="#3D5BA0" stroke-width="6"/>
    <path d="M 390 245 a 82 82 0 1 1 -8 -44" fill="none" stroke="#3D5BA0" stroke-width="5" opacity="0.7"/>
    <path d="M 383 235 a 48 48 0 1 1 -10 -28" fill="none" stroke="#3D5BA0" stroke-width="4" opacity="0.45"/>
    <text x="300" y="470" font-family="EB Garamond, serif" font-size="38" fill="#1B1611" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="600">find a protected eddy</text>
    <text x="300" y="520" font-family="EB Garamond, serif" font-size="30" fill="#7A6F5C" text-anchor="middle">a niche that doesn't scale — hold on a while longer</text>
  </g>
  <!-- right: wave -->
  <g>
    <path d="M 820 380 C 950 380, 1050 340, 1130 260 C 1190 200, 1230 150, 1260 120 C 1290 160, 1350 220, 1460 260"
          fill="none" stroke="#3F8278" stroke-width="7"/>
    <path d="M 820 420 C 970 420, 1090 390, 1190 330 C 1270 282, 1330 240, 1400 220"
          fill="none" stroke="#3F8278" stroke-width="5" opacity="0.55"/>
    <circle cx="1252" cy="128" r="12" fill="#BC4538"/>
    <text x="1140" y="470" font-family="EB Garamond, serif" font-size="38" fill="#1B1611" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="600">ride the wave</text>
    <text x="1140" y="520" font-family="EB Garamond, serif" font-size="30" fill="#7A6F5C" text-anchor="middle">become expert in scaling — and see what comes next</text>
  </g>
</svg>
```
:::

::: notes
And here is the honest framing of that choice, because I want to be careful: neither path is bad —
it depends on what you want. One real option: find a niche where things don't scale — where data is
scarce, where the loop runs through hardware, through a wet lab, through people — and hold on a
while longer. Those eddies exist and they are legitimate places to do beautiful science. The other:
use exactly this window to become an expert in scaling — in the meta-skill — and move with the wave
to see what comes next. What I'd argue against is only the default: drifting into one of these by
not choosing. Think about the futures you'd actually want to live in — including the uncomfortable
ones — so that you can genuinely advocate for what you want in the world.
:::


## Might as well enjoy it while the going's good {#close}

::: {style="text-align:center;margin-top:180px"}
[the last years of the old way · the first years of the new]{style="font-size:1.1em"}
:::

::: {style="text-align:center;margin-top:120px;color:#7A6F5C;font-size:0.8em"}
[cailmdaley.github.io/talks · lightconeresearch.github.io/agent-skills]{style="font-family:'IBM Plex Mono',monospace"}
:::

::: notes
I'll close where I started. We are living in the very last years of the old way of doing science
and the very first years of the new — and whatever else that is, it is not boring. The meta-skill
is temporary; the window is open now; and this combination — agentic modes of work pointed at real
physics by people with real taste — is going to produce some of the most fun and dramatic advances
astrophysics and ML have ever seen. So might as well enjoy it while the going's good. The tutorial
is at the link — run it this afternoon; it genuinely takes twenty minutes. And in a moment I'll
show you a live demo. Thank you.
:::

::: notes
Backup, for the verification discussion. [CNRS `#blinding`, Cail's script.] The discipline that
replaces a ground truth. Left: there's a truth, and the rest of the field clustered near it — and a
real pull to land your own result next to everyone else's. That pull is confirmation bias. Right: so
we blind ourselves — shift our number by a secret amount and hide where the field sits, so while we
make every analysis choice we genuinely can't tell how far we are from anyone. Only once every choice
is frozen do we unblind. For this room: it is exactly holding out a test set — you cannot tune toward
a number you cannot see. And note it composes with agents perfectly: the agent can make and record
every decision, and still never see the answer.
:::
